etymology: From elder, Old English eldra, an older or senior man, rendering Greek presbuteros; with qualification from Latin qualis, of what sort — the sort of man fit for the office.
biblical_def: The Spirit, through Paul, fixes the character of the man who may hold the office of elder, bishop, and overseer. Paul writes to Timothy at Ephesus, "A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach; Not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre; but patient, not a brawler, not covetous; One that ruleth well his own house, having his children in subjection with all gravity" (1 Tim 3:2–4). He adds, "Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil" (1 Tim 3:6). To Titus on Crete the same standard is repeated and grounded: such a man must be "blameless, as the steward of God" (Titus 1:7). The weight of the list is moral, not merely gifted: he must already govern his own household well before he is trusted with the household of God. The office is reserved to men — "the husband of one wife" — for the creational order set in Adam before the fall. Gifting without godliness disqualifies; a quarrelsome, drunken, or grasping man is barred though he preach ably. This dictionary confesses that Christ has appointed the qualifications of His undershepherds, and that a church which lowers them dishonours her Head.
webster_summary: The fixed scriptural requirements, chiefly of character, for the man who is set apart to the office of elder. They are given by Paul in his letters to Timothy and Titus, weigh moral fitness above natural ability, and restrict the office to qualified men.
webster_full: ELDER QUALIFICATIONS, noun. The scriptural marks of the man fit to hold the pastoral office of elder, bishop, and overseer.
Drawn chiefly from 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1, where the apostle Paul enumerates the character of the candidate.
"This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work" (1 Tim 3:1).
The list requires blamelessness, a single-minded husband of one wife, sobriety, aptness to teach, and rule of his own house; it forbids drunkenness, violence, greed, and novicehood.
It restricts the office to qualified men and binds the church to test the candidate by it before laying on of hands.
scriptures: 1 Tim 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
1 Tim 3:6
Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil.
Titus 1:6
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.
1 Tim 3:1
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
corruption_summary: The qualifications are quietly set aside wherever charisma, platform, or success is allowed to substitute for the proven character Scripture demands, and wherever the male-only standard is treated as a cultural relic.
corruption_paragraphs: The pressure of the age is to ordain by gifting and to overlook character — the dynamic preacher, the magnetic leader, the man who fills seats. Scripture inverts the priority: the one disputable qualification that is plainly a skill, "apt to teach," sits in a long list otherwise made of holiness, household, and self-government. A man may be eloquent and yet a brawler, greedy, or a recent convert puffed with pride; such a man is barred. Where churches measure elders by results rather than by 1 Timothy 3, they invite the very condemnation of the devil that Paul names.

A second corruption is to read "the husband of one wife" and the male office as bound culture rather than creational order. Paul grounds male headship in the church not in first-century Ephesus but in Adam formed first and Eve deceived (1 Tim 2:13–14). The qualifications therefore stand wherever the church stands: a sober, blameless, one-woman man who governs his home and is able to teach and to guard sound doctrine. To lower the bar is not mercy but rebellion against the Chief Shepherd who set it.
roots_summary: The English elder renders the Greek presbuteros, a senior man, identified in Scripture with the episkopos or overseer.
roots_lines: Greek presbuteros, an older man, gives our word presbyter and stands behind elder.
Greek episkopos, overseer, is rendered bishop and names the same office (Titus 1:5,7).
The two titles are interchanged in one breath, proving one office, not a hierarchy of ranks.
Hebrew zaqen, the elder at the gate, supplies the Old Testament background of governing seniority.
Qualification, from Latin qualis, asks not how able but of what sort the man is.
usage: He preached well, but the session weighed him against the elder qualifications and found him a novice.
Sound elder qualifications guard the flock by testing a man's home before trusting him with the church.
The elder qualifications are not suggestions but the standing law of Christ for His undershepherds.

etymology: From Greek anepilemptos (1 Tim 3:2), "not able to be laid hold of," and anenkletos (Titus 1:6), "not arraigned"; rendered blameless, from Old English blame through Latin blasphemare.
biblical_def: Above reproach is the overarching qualification under which every other mark of the elder gathers. Paul opens the list with it: "A bishop then must be blameless" (1 Tim 3:2), and to Titus, "If any be blameless" (Titus 1:6), repeating it as he names the office, "For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God" (Titus 1:7). The Greek anepilemptos pictures a man who offers no handle, no projecting hook by which an accuser may seize and drag him; anenkletos pictures a man against whom no charge can be made to stick in court. The word does not mean sinless — no man this side of glory is that — but it means without scandal, without a settled and visible blot that would shame the gospel and silence his rebuke of others. The deacon too must be "found blameless" after proving (1 Tim 3:10). Such a life is the soil in which all the particular virtues grow: hospitality, sobriety, gentleness, and aptness to teach are the shape that blamelessness takes. This dictionary confesses that Christ requires of His overseers a life that gives the watching world and the accusing devil no purchase, that the name of God be not blasphemed through His ministers.
webster_summary: The chief and summary qualification of an elder: a life so ordered that no accusation can take hold. It renders the Greek anepilemptos and anenkletos, meaning not sinless but without settled scandal, and it governs all the particular virtues that follow.
webster_full: ABOVE REPROACH, adjective. Blameless; offering no handle by which an accuser may lay hold.
It translates the apostle's anepilemptos and anenkletos, the heading qualification of the bishop and the deacon.
"A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober" (1 Tim 3:2).
It requires not perfection but the absence of any open and disqualifying blot upon the man's name and walk.
It is the root from which hospitality, sobriety, and aptness to teach grow as its branches.
scriptures: 1 Tim 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Titus 1:6
If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.
Titus 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
And let these also first be proved; then let them use the office of a deacon, being found blameless.
corruption_summary: Blamelessness is hollowed out where reputation is managed rather than character formed, and where a settled scandal is excused as a private matter that need not touch a man's public office.
corruption_paragraphs: The age prizes image over integrity, the curated reputation over the proven walk. But anepilemptos asks whether there is in fact a hook to be grasped, not merely whether the man has hidden it well. A church satisfied with the appearance of blamelessness, while tolerating known and unrepented sin in its officers, has not kept the qualification but counterfeited it. The remedy is the apostolic order: "let these also first be proved" (1 Tim 3:10) — tested in the open over time, not waved through on charm.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that blamelessness is the indispensable platform for rebuke. An elder must "by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers" (Titus 1:9); a man with an open blot cannot wield the sword, for his own life answers him. The church should therefore prize quiet, long-tested faithfulness in her candidates above brilliance, knowing that a blameless walk lends weight to every word.
roots_summary: The term gathers two Greek words, anepilemptos and anenkletos, both prefixed with the negative a-, denying any grip or charge against the man.
roots_lines: Greek anepilemptos (1 Tim 3:2): not epilambano, not able to be laid hold of.
Greek anenkletos (Titus 1:6): not enkaleo, not called into court or arraigned.
The negative prefix a- in both denies, not the existence of sin, but the existence of a disqualifying handle.
English blameless traces through Latin blasphemare, the very evil a scandalous officer invites (1 Tim 6:1).
The legal flavour of anenkletos recalls the courtroom: no charge can be made to stand.
usage: The candidate was gifted, but he was not above reproach, and the elders rightly delayed his ordination.
To be above reproach is not to be sinless but to give the accuser no handle to seize.
An officer above reproach can rebuke the gainsayer, for his own walk does not answer him back.

etymology: From Latin pastor, a shepherd, from pascere, to feed; the pastor is the shepherd set by Christ to feed His flock.
biblical_def: The pastoral office is the work of the shepherd-teacher whom the ascended Christ gives to His church. Among His ascension gifts Paul lists "pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ" (Eph 4:11–12). The office is one with that of elder, bishop, and overseer; Peter joins all three in one charge: "The elders which are among you I exhort... Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof" (1 Pet 5:1–2). The shepherd's threefold labour is to feed the flock by the word, to lead the flock by example and government, and to guard the flock from wolves — for Paul warned the Ephesian elders, "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood" (Acts 20:28). Every such man is an undershepherd, accountable to the Chief Shepherd who will appear: "when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away" (1 Pet 5:4). This dictionary confesses the pastoral office as Christ's own institution, not a human profession, by which He continues to feed and keep His blood-bought flock.
webster_summary: The shepherding office given by the ascended Christ, identical with that of elder and overseer. Its work is to feed, lead, and guard the flock by the word, under the Chief Shepherd to whom every pastor must give account.
webster_full: THE PASTORAL OFFICE, noun. The shepherd-teacher's charge over the flock of God.
An ascension gift of Christ (Eph 4:11), identical with the office of elder, bishop, and overseer.
"Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof" (1 Pet 5:2).
It requires the pastor to feed by the word, to lead by example and government, and to guard against wolves.
It makes him an undershepherd, accountable to the Chief Shepherd at His appearing.
scriptures: Eph 4:11
And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers;
1 Pet 5:2
Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;
Acts 20:28
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
1 Pet 5:4
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: The pastoral office is corrupted where the shepherd is recast as a chief executive, a brand, or a therapist, and where feeding and guarding the flock give way to managing an institution.
corruption_paragraphs: Much of the visible church has traded the shepherd for the entrepreneur. The pastor becomes a vision-caster, a brand, a manager of programmes and budgets, and the sheep become an audience to be retained. But the office is shepherdly: to feed with the word, to know and lead the flock, and to stand between the sheep and the wolf. Paul wept over the Ephesians because "grievous wolves" would enter (Acts 20:29); a hireling who flees danger, or who never names it, has abandoned the office while keeping the title.

A subtler corruption recasts the pastor as therapist, the pulpit as a place to soothe felt needs rather than to feed and to guard. Yet the flock is fed only by truth, and guarded only by warning. The recovery is to remember whose flock it is: Christ "purchased" the church "with his own blood" (Acts 20:28), and every pastor is His undershepherd, who will answer to the Chief Shepherd. That accountability dignifies the office and forbids its reduction to management or comfort.
roots_summary: Pastor is simply the Latin word for shepherd, and the office is everywhere drawn from the shepherding imagery of Scripture.
roots_lines: Latin pastor, shepherd, from pascere, to feed — the pastor's first work.
Greek poimen, shepherd, is the word in Ephesians 4:11 rendered pastor.
Hebrew ra'ah, to shepherd, describes the LORD Himself in Psalm 23 and David in 2 Samuel 5.
Greek episkopos, overseer, names the same man under the aspect of oversight (1 Pet 5:2).
Christ is the archipoimen, the Chief Shepherd, of whom every pastor is an undershepherd (1 Pet 5:4).
usage: He understood the pastoral office as feeding and guarding the flock, not building a platform.
The pastoral office binds a man to the Chief Shepherd, before whom he must give account for every soul.
Wolves test the pastoral office, for the hireling flees but the true shepherd stands.

etymology: From pastoral (Latin pastor, shepherd) and epistle (Greek epistole, a letter sent); so named because they instruct Christ's shepherds in ordering His church.
biblical_def: The Pastoral Epistles are the three letters of Paul to two pastors — First and Second Timothy and Titus — in which the apostle instructs his sons in the faith on church order, qualified men, and sound doctrine. They open with Paul's own name and apostolic claim: "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 1:1); "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God" (2 Tim 1:1); "Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ" (Titus 1:1). Here Christ gives the church her standing manual for appointing elders and deacons, setting the qualifications, charging the public reading and preaching of the word, and guarding the deposit of truth against false teachers. The critical academy advances the theory that these letters are pseudonymous — forged in Paul's name by a later hand — pointing to vocabulary and church structure. This dictionary rejects that theory as both unproven and corrosive: a forged letter that says "I Paul" (compare 2 Tim 1:1) is a lie, and the Spirit does not inspire lies. The early church received all three as Pauline, and the internal claims, personal greetings, and travel notices are the marks of genuine apostolic correspondence. This dictionary confesses these three letters as the inspired, Pauline, and authoritative charter of the pastoral office.
webster_summary: The three New Testament letters of Paul to Timothy and Titus, instructing pastors in church order, qualified officers, and sound doctrine. Their Pauline authorship is affirmed against the critical theory that they were forged under his name.
webster_full: THE PASTORAL EPISTLES, noun. The three Pauline letters to Timothy and Titus on the ordering of the church.
They comprise First Timothy, Second Timothy, and Titus, each opening with Paul's name and apostolic claim.
"Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour" (1 Tim 1:1).
They supply the qualifications of elders and deacons, the charge to preach, and the guard of sound doctrine.
Their genuine Pauline authorship is confessed against the academy's theory of pseudonymous forgery.
scriptures: 1 Tim 1:1
Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the commandment of God our Saviour, and Lord Jesus Christ, which is our hope;
2 Tim 1:1
Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, according to the promise of life which is in Christ Jesus,
Titus 1:1
Paul, a servant of God, and an apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of God's elect, and the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness;
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: The chief assault on these letters is the historical-critical theory of pseudonymity, which holds them to be later forgeries falsely signed with Paul's name — a theory this dictionary rejects as unproven and as making the Spirit the author of a lie.
corruption_paragraphs: The academy teaches that the Pastorals are pseudonymous: written after Paul's death by an admirer who borrowed his name, alleging that their vocabulary, their settled church offices, and their warnings against error point to a later age. The argument fails on its own terms. Word-counts across three short personal letters prove nothing about authorship; elders and deacons appear already in Acts and Philippians within Paul's lifetime; and false teaching was present from the first. More gravely, the theory cannot be squared with inspiration. A letter that declares "Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ" (2 Tim 1:1) and sends personal greetings is either true or a forgery; there is no innocent ancient convention that turns "I Paul" into honest fiction when the Holy Ghost is the author.

The early church knew the difference between genuine and spurious writings and received these three as Paul's without dispute, while rejecting actual forgeries. To grant the critical theory is to surrender 2 Timothy 3:16 in the very letter that asserts it. The recovery is plain confession: these are the words of the apostle Paul, breathed out by God, and therefore the binding charter for ordering Christ's church in every age.
roots_summary: The name joins pastoral, of the shepherd, with epistle, a sent letter, marking these as Paul's shepherding correspondence to his fellow shepherds.
roots_lines: Epistle, from Greek epistole, a letter dispatched to a person or church.
Pastoral, from Latin pastor, shepherd, because the letters equip shepherds of the flock.
The title is a later convenience; the letters themselves name only their author, Paul, and their recipients.
Timothy was Paul's "own son in the faith" (1 Tim 1:2); Titus, "mine own son after the common faith" (Titus 1:4).
The contested word pseudonymous means falsely-named — precisely the charge this dictionary denies.
usage: He preached through the Pastoral Epistles to teach the young congregation how Christ would have His church ordered.
The Pastoral Epistles give the elder his qualifications and the church her marching orders for sound doctrine.
We affirm the Pastoral Epistles as genuinely Pauline, against every theory of later forgery.

etymology: From preach, Latin praedicare, to proclaim publicly, rendering Greek kerusso, to herald; the herald cries the word of his King.
biblical_def: Preach the word is the dying charge of Paul to Timothy and the standing commission of every pastor. In his last letter the apostle solemnly binds his son in the faith: "I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:1–2). The verb is kerusso, to herald — the preacher is not a lecturer offering opinions but a herald crying the King's decree, and the content is fixed: "the word," the inspired Scripture, not the herald's own wit. Paul foresees the reason for so urgent a charge: "For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2 Tim 4:3). The remedy for itching ears is not a different message but the faithful one, pressed in season and out, with reproof, rebuke, and exhortation. This is expository fidelity — the opening and applying of the text — over against entertainment, felt-need talks, and the marketing of the pulpit to consumer appetite. This dictionary confesses that preaching is the heralded word of God, and that a church starved of it, however entertained, is famished.
webster_summary: Paul's solemn charge to herald the inspired Scripture in season and out, with reproof, rebuke, and exhortation. It establishes expository fidelity to the text against entertainment and felt-need preaching.
webster_full: PREACH THE WORD, verb phrase. To herald the inspired Scripture as the fixed content of the pulpit.
The dying charge of Paul to Timothy, sworn before God and the judging Christ (2 Tim 4:1).
"Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:2).
It requires the herald's urgency and the text's authority, against the lectures of mere opinion.
It forbids the trading of the word for entertainment to please itching ears (2 Tim 4:3).
scriptures: 2 Tim 4:2
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
2 Tim 4:1
I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom;
2 Tim 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher?
corruption_summary: Preaching is corrupted wherever the herald's fixed word is swapped for entertainment, felt-need talks, and consumer-driven content designed to soothe rather than to reprove and exhort.
corruption_paragraphs: The market church has rebuilt the pulpit around the listener's appetite. Topical talks address felt needs, stories and stagecraft replace exposition, and the sermon is engineered to be inoffensive and brief. This is precisely the apostasy Paul predicted: a generation that "will not endure sound doctrine" and gathers teachers to scratch its "itching ears" (2 Tim 4:3). The error is not in clear communication but in the surrender of the content — "the word" — to the hearer's wishes. A herald who softens the King's decree to keep the crowd has ceased to herald.

The recovery is expository fidelity: to open the text, declare its meaning, and press its reproof, rebuke, and exhortation upon the conscience "with all longsuffering and doctrine" (2 Tim 4:2). Faith comes by hearing the word (Rom 10:17), and souls are fed and saved by the heralded Scripture, not by performance. The pulpit is therefore to be reformed back to the word — in season when it is welcome, out of season when it is not.
roots_summary: The phrase rests on the verb kerusso, to herald, and on the object "the word," the inspired Scripture proclaimed.
roots_lines: Greek kerusso, to herald, pictures the public crier announcing his king's decree.
The noun keryx, herald, marks the preacher's office as proclamation, not opinion.
"The word," Greek logos, fixes the content as the inspired Scripture, not the speaker's wit.
Latin praedicare, to proclaim before, gives our English preach and predicate.
Instant renders ephistemi, to stand ready upon — the herald always at his post.
usage: Charged to preach the word, he opened the text rather than telling stories to fill the hour.
When the people would not endure sound doctrine, he obeyed the charge to preach the word the more.
To preach the word is to herald the King's decree, in season and out, whether it is welcomed or refused.

etymology: From Latin admonere, to put in mind, to warn; rendering Greek noutheteo, to place in the mind, to warn and instruct.
biblical_def: To admonish is to warn and instruct, setting truth before the mind so as to turn a man from sin and folly. The Greek noutheteo joins nous, the mind, with tithemi, to place — to put a thing in someone's mind. Paul makes it the heart of his own ministry: "Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28), where "warning" is this very word. It is first a pastoral labour: the Thessalonians are told to "know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you" (1 Thess 5:12). Yet it is not the pastor's alone, for the same letter charges the whole body, "warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14), and Paul commends the Roman saints as "able also to admonish one another" (Rom 15:14). Admonition is therefore both an office-duty of elders and a mutual duty of the saints, always governed by love and aimed at recovery, not by harshness. This dictionary confesses admonition as an ordinary means by which Christ keeps His people, warning the unruly and instructing the wandering until every man is presented perfect in Him.
webster_summary: To warn and instruct, placing truth before the mind to turn a man from sin. It renders the Greek noutheteo, is a pastoral duty toward the unruly, and is also commanded among all the saints toward one another.
webster_full: ADMONISH, verb transitive. To warn and instruct; to set truth before the mind for correction.
It renders the Greek noutheteo, from nous, the mind, and is the heart of Paul's own ministry.
"Warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28).
It is required of elders who are "over you in the Lord" (1 Thess 5:12), warning the unruly.
It is also a mutual duty of the saints, "able also to admonish one another" (Rom 15:14).
scriptures: Col 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
And I myself also am persuaded of you, my brethren, that ye also are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to admonish one another.
1 Thess 5:12
And we beseech you, brethren, to know them which labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you;
1 Thess 5:14
Now we exhort you, brethren, warn them that are unruly, comfort the feebleminded, support the weak, be patient toward all men.
corruption_summary: Admonition is resisted in an age that treats all warning as judgmentalism, and it is also distorted where it is severed from love and aimed at wounding rather than recovering the wanderer.
corruption_paragraphs: The spirit of the age forbids warning altogether, branding every loving rebuke as judgmental, intolerant, or unkind. But Paul makes admonition the very work of gospel ministry, "warning every man... that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus" (Col 1:28). To withhold the warning a brother needs is not love but cruelty dressed as tolerance. The church that will not admonish abandons the unruly to their sin and forfeits an ordinary means by which Christ keeps His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the patient, mutual character of admonition: it is to be done "in all wisdom" (Col 1:28) and with patience "toward all men" (1 Thess 5:14), by elders set over the flock and by saints toward one another. It aims always at the man's recovery, not his humiliation. A church rich in loving admonition is a church that guards its members; a church that has lost it grows soft toward sin.
roots_summary: The English admonish renders the Greek noutheteo, to place in the mind, the activity of warning instruction.
roots_lines: Greek noutheteo, from nous (mind) and tithemi (to place): to put a thing in the mind.
The noun nouthesia, admonition, names the loving warning itself (Eph 6:4).
Latin admonere, to put in mind, to warn, gives our English admonish and monitor.
The word carries both warning and instruction; it confronts error and supplies truth at once.
It is governed throughout Scripture by love, patience, and the aim of recovery (1 Thess 5:14).
usage: He did not scold the wanderer but went to admonish him, setting Scripture plainly before his mind.
Paul charges every saint to admonish one another, not the pastor alone.
To admonish the unruly is an act of love, for it warns a brother off the path to ruin.

etymology: Rendering Greek allelon, of one another, the reciprocal pronoun marking the mutual duties of the members of Christ's body.
biblical_def: The "one anothers" are the reciprocal commands of the New Testament — love one another, forbear one another, exhort one another, serve one another, prefer one another — that describe the mutual life of the body of Christ. The word is allelon, recurring scores of times. Paul gathers many in one place: "Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another... distributing to the necessity of saints" (Rom 12:10,13), and earlier, "we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another" (Rom 12:5). To the Ephesians he writes, "Forbearing one another in love; Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Eph 4:2–3), and to the Thessalonians, "comfort yourselves together, and edify one another" (1 Thess 5:11). These mutual duties are the warm and ordinary fabric of congregational life. Yet they do not level the offices Christ has set: the same Paul who commands mutual submission also commands wives to submit to husbands and the flock to obey their elders. The body has many members of differing function, "not... the same office" (Rom 12:4). This dictionary confesses the one anothers as the genuine reciprocity of love within the church, lived out under, not against, the order of headship and office that God has appointed.
webster_summary: The reciprocal commands of the New Testament — to love, forbear, exhort, serve, and prefer one another — describing the mutual life of Christ's body. They are real reciprocity in love, yet do not abolish the differing offices God has set.
webster_full: ONE ANOTHER, noun phrase. The reciprocal duties of the members of Christ's body.
Rendering the Greek allelon, gathered richly in Romans 12, Ephesians 4, and the Thessalonian letters.
"Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another" (Rom 12:10).
It requires the mutual love, forbearance, exhortation, and service of all the saints.
It does not level the offices of the church but is lived under the order God has set.
scriptures: Be kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another;
Eph 4:2
With all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love;
1 Thess 5:11
Wherefore comfort yourselves together, and edify one another, even as also ye do.
Rom 12:5
So we, being many, are one body in Christ, and every one members one of another.
corruption_summary: The one anothers are abused where "mutuality" is made to abolish office and headship, as though reciprocal love and ordained authority could not stand together in the same body.
corruption_paragraphs: A levelling reading seizes the one anothers — especially "submitting yourselves one to another" (Eph 5:21) — to argue that Scripture knows no fixed office, no male eldership, no headship in the home, only undifferentiated equals. But the very passages that command mutual duty also command particular order: the same context that says "submitting yourselves one to another" goes on to direct wives, children, and servants specifically (Eph 5:22ff). Paul's image is a body of many members with differing functions, "not... the same office" (Rom 12:4). Reciprocal love does not dissolve appointed authority; it adorns it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that the church is a true family, not a mere institution: its members are "members one of another" (Rom 12:5), bound to love, forbear, comfort, and edify in a hundred ordinary acts. The recovery of the one anothers cures both a cold, transactional churchmanship and a flattening egalitarianism — for warm mutual love and ordained office are not rivals but companions in the one body.
roots_summary: The phrase renders the single Greek reciprocal pronoun allelon, of one another, which threads the apostolic letters.
roots_lines: Greek allelon, the reciprocal pronoun, recurs roughly fifty times across the New Testament.
It governs verbs of love, forbearance, exhortation, service, and honour among the saints.
Romans 12, Ephesians 4, and 1 Thessalonians gather many of these duties in close compass.
The body image (Rom 12:4–5) frames mutuality without erasing differing function.
English one another simply distributes the reciprocity across the members of the body.
usage: The church practised the one anothers, bearing one another's burdens without erasing the elders' office.
He showed how the one another commands warm a congregation without levelling the order God set.
To love one another is no rival to honouring those over you in the Lord; both are commanded.

etymology: From sound, healthy or whole, rendering Greek hugiaino (whence English hygiene); with doctrine, Latin doctrina, teaching — healthful teaching.
biblical_def: Sound doctrine is healthful, health-giving teaching — the apostolic deposit of truth that nourishes the soul and is to be guarded against novelty and error. The Greek is hugiainousa didaskalia, from hugiaino, to be healthy, the root of our word hygiene; doctrine is "sound" as a body is sound, whole and free of disease. Paul sets the law against "whatsoever else is contrary to sound doctrine" (1 Tim 1:10), and warns Timothy of the day "when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears" (2 Tim 4:3). The elder is required to be one "holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers" (Titus 1:9), and Titus himself is charged, "But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine" (Titus 2:1). Sound doctrine is therefore not bare orthodoxy but living truth that produces godliness; error sickens, but truth heals. It is a fixed deposit, "the faithful word," to be held fast, taught, and defended, not revised to suit the appetite of the hour. This dictionary confesses sound doctrine as the healthful teaching of Scripture, by which Christ feeds His flock and arms His elders against every gainsayer.
webster_summary: Healthful, health-giving teaching — the fixed apostolic deposit of truth that nourishes godliness. It renders the Greek hugiainousa didaskalia, is to be held fast and taught by elders, and is guarded against novelty and error.
webster_full: SOUND DOCTRINE, noun. Healthful teaching; the wholesome deposit of apostolic truth.
It renders the Greek hugiainousa didaskalia, doctrine sound as a body is whole and free of disease.
"Speak thou the things which become sound doctrine" (Titus 2:1).
It equips the elder "by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers" (Titus 1:9).
It is guarded against the itching ears that "will not endure sound doctrine" (2 Tim 4:3).
scriptures: For whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine;
2 Tim 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
Titus 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Titus 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
corruption_summary: Sound doctrine is corrupted wherever truth is treated as endlessly revisable to suit the appetite of the age, and wherever doctrine itself is despised as divisive in favour of vague sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: The age prizes novelty and despises the fixed. It heaps up teachers who say what itching ears wish to hear, and it dismisses doctrine as cold, divisive, or unloving compared with experience and sentiment. But Paul calls doctrine healthful: as a sound body needs wholesome food, the soul needs wholesome teaching. The teaching that flatters the lusts of the hour is not a kinder doctrine but a sickly one, and the churches that feast on it grow spiritually diseased even while they feel affirmed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is that doctrine is for life: sound teaching produces godliness, and the elder is to wield it "both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers" (Titus 1:9). The recovery is to hold fast the faithful word as a fixed deposit, to teach it plainly, and to defend it boldly, knowing that truth heals where error sickens, and that love for souls demands the sound doctrine, not the sweet poison.
roots_summary: The English "sound" renders the Greek hugiaino, to be healthy, joined to didaskalia, teaching — healthful teaching.
roots_lines: Greek hugiaino, to be healthy or whole, gives our word hygiene.
Greek didaskalia, teaching or instruction, from didasko, to teach.
Together hugiainousa didaskalia, health-giving teaching, the phrase rendered "sound doctrine."
English sound, whole or healthy, as in a sound body or a sound foundation.
Latin doctrina, instruction, from docere, to teach, gives doctrine and doctor.
usage: He spoke the things that become sound doctrine, refusing to trim the truth to itching ears.
Sound doctrine is healthful, feeding the soul as wholesome food feeds the body.
An elder armed with sound doctrine can both exhort the saints and convince the gainsayers.

etymology: From king, Old English cyning, ruler; and priest, Greek presbuteros through Latin presbyter; the distinction of crown and altar under the old covenant.
biblical_def: Under the old covenant God set a wall between the office of king and the office of priest, that no man might join in himself the crown and the altar — until Christ, of whom both spoke, should unite them in His own person. King Uzziah of Judah, "when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense" (2 Chr 26:16). Fourscore priests withstood him, saying, "It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense" (2 Chr 26:18). The king raged, "and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead" (2 Chr 26:19), and he was a leper to his death, cut off from the house of the LORD. The crown was of Judah, the altar of Aaron and Levi; the two were not to be confounded. Yet the prophet foresaw their union: "he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13). This is fulfilled only in Christ, a priest after the order of Melchizedek, who is "King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace" (Heb 7:2). This dictionary confesses that the old-covenant separation of offices guarded the holiness of God and pointed forward to the one Mediator, our King and Priest, the Lord Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: The old-covenant separation of the kingly and priestly offices, dramatized in Uzziah's leprosy when he usurped the altar. The two offices were kept apart until Christ, priest after Melchizedek, lawfully unites crown and altar in Himself.
webster_full: KING AND PRIEST, noun. The distinction of the royal and priestly offices under the old covenant.
Dramatized in King Uzziah, struck with leprosy for usurping the priests' work of burning incense.
"It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron" (2 Chr 26:18).
It kept the crown of Judah and the altar of Aaron apart, that the holiness of God be guarded.
It is resolved only in Christ, who "shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13; Heb 7).
scriptures: But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense.

Then Uzziah was wroth, and had a censer in his hand to burn incense: and while he was wroth with the priests, the leprosy even rose up in his forehead before the priests in the house of the LORD, from beside the incense altar.
Zech 6:13

Even he shall build the temple of the LORD; and he shall bear the glory, and shall sit and rule upon his throne; and he shall be a priest upon his throne: and the counsel of peace shall be between them both.
Heb 7:2
To whom also Abraham gave a tenth part of all; first being by interpretation King of righteousness, and after that also King of Salem, which is, King of peace;
corruption_summary: The lesson of the distinction is lost wherever men presume to seize an office God has not given them, blurring the lines of authority that Scripture and Christ's order set.
corruption_paragraphs: Uzziah's sin was presumption: strong and successful, his heart was lifted up, and he reached for an office that was not his. The standing warning is against any usurpation of God-appointed office — whether the magistrate intruding upon the things of God, or, in the church, those who grasp at an office Christ has not conferred. The Roman papacy provides a grave instance, claiming both temporal and spiritual supremacy in one man, a confounding of crown and altar that Scripture never grants to any but Christ. God guards the boundaries of office, and He humbles those who leap them, as Uzziah was made a leper to his death.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is the glory of Christ, in whom the two offices are at last lawfully one. The old covenant kept king and priest apart precisely to magnify the wonder that the Branch "shall be a priest upon his throne" (Zech 6:13). He alone, a priest after Melchizedek who needs no Aaronic descent, rules and intercedes together; and so the very separation that condemned Uzziah exalts the Lord Jesus, our King and our Priest forever.
roots_summary: The distinction sets the royal line of Judah apart from the priestly line of Aaron, two offices joined only in the antitype, Christ after the order of Melchizedek.
roots_lines: Hebrew melek, king, of the tribe of Judah; the throne was not Levitical.
Hebrew kohen, priest, of the sons of Aaron and the tribe of Levi; the altar was not royal.
Uzziah's name means "the LORD is my strength," the very strength that lifted his heart to ruin.
Melchizedek, "king of righteousness" and "king of Salem," held both offices as a type (Heb 7:1–2).
The Branch of Zechariah 6:13 unites throne and altar, fulfilled in Christ alone.
usage: He cited the king-priest distinction to show why no mere man may claim both crown and altar.
Uzziah's leprosy teaches the king-priest distinction: God humbles those who seize an office not their own.
Only in Christ is the king-priest distinction lawfully resolved, for He is priest upon His throne.

etymology: From Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD is gracious"; surnamed the Baptist, Greek baptistes, from baptizo, to immerse, for the baptism of repentance he administered.
biblical_def: John the Baptist was the forerunner of the Lord Jesus Christ, the last and greatest of the prophets of the old covenant, sent to prepare His way. He is the voice foretold by Isaiah: "The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD" (Isa 40:3), and the messenger of Malachi, "Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me" (Mal 3:1). He came preaching "in the wilderness of Judaea... Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt 3:1–2), and baptized with the baptism of repentance, requiring fruits meet for repentance and pointing beyond himself to the Lamb of God. When his disciples grew jealous for him, John spoke the model words of every true minister: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). Of him the Lord testified, "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he" (Matt 11:11) — greatest as the herald who stood at the threshold of the new covenant, yet less in privilege than the humblest believer who stands within it, knowing the finished work of Christ. He sealed his witness in martyrdom under Herod. This dictionary confesses John as the faithful forerunner whose whole greatness lay in pointing away from himself to the Christ.
webster_summary: The forerunner of Christ, last of the old-covenant prophets, who preached the baptism of repentance and pointed to the Lamb of God. Christ called him the greatest born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater than he.
webster_full: JOHN THE BAPTIST, proper noun. The forerunner of Christ and last of the prophets before the gospel.
Foretold by Isaiah and Malachi as the voice and messenger preparing the LORD's way.
"Repent ye: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" (Matt 3:2), preaching the baptism of repentance.
He pointed wholly away from himself: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).
Christ named him greatest of those born of women, yet the least in the kingdom is greater (Matt 11:11).
scriptures: Isa 40:3
The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
Mal 3:1

Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.
John 3:30
He must increase, but I must decrease.
Matt 11:11
Verily I say unto you, Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist: notwithstanding he that is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he.
corruption_summary: John's witness is distorted wherever his baptism of repentance is detached from his testimony to Christ, or wherever a minister inverts his rule and seeks to increase while Christ decreases.
corruption_paragraphs: Some have made too much of the man and too little of his message, gathering as disciples of John rather than passing through him to Christ — an error already met in Acts, where men who knew "only the baptism of John" were brought on to faith in the Lord Jesus (Acts 19:3–5). John would have none of it; his whole greatness lay in self-effacement, "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30). The minister who builds a following to himself, who increases while Christ is obscured, has reversed the forerunner's rule and forfeited his glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The positive principle to recover is John's model of ministry: a voice, not the Word; a friend of the Bridegroom who rejoices to hear His voice; a herald content to fade as the Sun rises. Every preacher and every saint is called to John's posture — to point away from self to the Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world, and to count it joy to decrease that Christ may increase.
roots_summary: His name means "the LORD is gracious," and his surname, the Baptist, comes from the immersing baptism of repentance he administered.
roots_lines: Hebrew Yochanan, "the LORD is gracious," the meaning of John's name.
Greek baptistes, Baptist, from baptizo, to immerse, marks his baptism of repentance.
Isaiah's "voice... in the wilderness" (40:3) names his office as forerunner.
Malachi's "my messenger" (3:1) foretells the herald before the Lord's coming.
"He must decrease" (John 3:30) fixes his place: all greatness in pointing to Christ.
usage: John the Baptist cried in the wilderness, preparing the way of the Lord he was sent to herald.
The pastor took John the Baptist as his pattern: he must increase, but I must decrease.
Greatest of the prophets, John the Baptist still counted the least believer in the kingdom greater than he.
